articles.title: Bipartisan lawmakers press Hegseth to expand Ukraine’s access to Starshield
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of House and Senate lawmakers is pressing the Trump administration to restore and expand Ukraine’s access to Starshield satellite systems, warning that a failure to do so will cripple Kyiv’s military operations against Russia. In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the lawmakers — all of them staunch Ukraine allies —…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of House and Senate lawmakers is pressing the Trump administration to restore and expand Ukraine’s access to Starshield satellite systems, warning that a failure to do so will cripple Kyiv’s military operations against Russia.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the lawmakers — all of them staunch Ukraine allies — urged the administration not only to lift any speed restrictions related to the systems, but also to expand the Starshield contract to bolster Ukraine’s military capacity, even over Russian territory.

“Ukrainian forces depend on these services for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications, and the operation of unmanned systems,” the lawmakers wrote. “Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine’s military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm’s way.”

The letter was signed by three senators — Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) — and five members of the House: Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio), Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), Jim Costa (D-Calif.) and Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.).

The push is just the latest part of a broader outcry on Capitol Hill over reports that Starshield’s receivers quit working earlier this month for Ukrainian military equipment operating above a certain speed. Starshield is a specialized branch of the Starlink satellite systems run by SpaceX, which is owned by tech mogul Elon Musk.

Musk has said any decisions to restrict Starshield were not his and must have come from President Trump and the Pentagon. A recent report by The Wall Street Journal , however, contradicted that account, saying Musk was behind the restrictions. The report infuriated many lawmakers in the Capitol, who say decisions affecting the military capability of Ukraine — or any U.S. ally — should not be left in the hands of any single company.

“Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine’s ability to defend itself,” the bipartisan group wrote to Hegseth.

Trump on Thursday said his administration had contacted Musk, who in turn restored the Starshield services to Ukraine. But Ukrainian officials on Friday said the systems were still not functioning.

The issue has emerged on the campaign trail in the final weeks before the midterms, with Democrats accusing Trump and Musk, a major GOP donor, of cozying up to Russia at the expense of a democratic ally.

The topic is also likely to resurface in the lame-duck session, as some House Republicans are already warning GOP leaders that they’re ready to block their party’s legislative agenda unless the administration reverses course and lends more help to Ukraine.

In their letter, the bipartisan Ukraine allies offered one idea for how Hegseth could do so: They want Defense Department officials to use their unilateral powers under the Defense Production Act “to prioritize the provision and expansion of satellite communications services necessary to support Ukraine’s defense.”

“These authorities should be considered alongside existing contractual mechanisms to ensure that Ukraine maintains reliable access to the bandwidth, service levels, and geographic coverage required for its lawful military operations,” the lawmakers wrote. “Ensuring reliable access to satellite communications is essential to sustaining Ukraine’s defense and protecting U.S. national security interests.”

articles.title: Acton’s mother was convicted of theft, animal cruelty: What to know
articles.summary: A GOP campaign ad featuring the estranged mother of Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) received blowback this week after it was revealed Acton’s mother stood by her husband after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton as a child. Court records show that the mother, Donna Arthur, has faced legal troubles of her own,…
articles.body:
A GOP campaign ad featuring the estranged mother of Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D) received blowback this week after it was revealed Acton’s mother stood by her husband after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton as a child.

Court records show that the mother, Donna Arthur, has faced legal troubles of her own, with convictions related to theft and animal cruelty, according to public legal filings Acton’s campaign has shared with The Hill.

In April 2021, Arthur was charged in Pennsylvania with neglecting animals after a judge found she kept several cats in a “locked and filthy vehicle” with an internal temperature of 120 degrees.

Upon appeal, a higher court vacated her sentence and conviction in 2023 after it determined the trial court made an error when it failed to assess Arthur’s right to counsel.

Previously, Arthur pleaded guilty in a 1995 case in which she was charged with passing bad checks and theft by deception or false impression. She was found guilty on similar charges a year later and sentenced to a maximum of two years in prison, although it’s unclear how much of this sentence she served.

GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign has claimed credit for and defended the controversial ad featuring Arthur, in which she calls her daughter a “liar” and urges Ohioans to vote against her in the November election.

Acton previously disclosed during a 2019 interview with The Vindicator that she had experienced abuse, neglect and a period of homelessness while living with her mother after her parents’ divorce.

Acton told the outlet she was also sexually abused by Arthur’s husband, who was indicted on rape charges in 1978. The Democrat said the last time she saw her mother was at the courthouse when her stepfather was arrested, saying Arthur “turned her cheek away” when she tried to give her a kiss.

The candidate’s brother, Philip Stearns, criticized Ramaswamy for the video in a campaign ad released Tuesday afternoon.

“Shame on Vivek,” Stearns said. “It’s the contempt he has for Amy. It’s the contempt he has for Ohio. He’s not fit to lead.”

President Trump and Vice President Vance defended Ramaswamy from criticism about the ad this week, while Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) and his predecessor John Kasich (R) have called on Ramaswamy to take down the ad.

After NBC News reporter Monica Alba pressed the president outside the White House on Friday about the allegations of sexual assault made against Acton’s stepfather, Trump told her to be “quiet” and praised Arthur as a “smart person.”

“This has nothing to do with the stepfather or anything else,” the president said. “This has to do with the fact that a woman got out, the mother of a person running for governor … said that she’s a liar, her daughter’s a liar.”

Trump added he believed Arthur’s comments were “very much fair game.”

The Hill has reached out to the Ramaswamy campaign about the new revelations about Arthur’s legal troubles.

articles.title: Focus groups: Their candidates lost in the Michigan and Texas primaries. Now what?
articles.summary: Some voters who backed losing candidates in two key Senate primaries this year are still wrestling with whether to support their party’s nominee on Election Day, with massive implications for who controls the Senate majority next year.
articles.body: Some voters who backed losing candidates in two key Senate primaries this year are still wrestling with whether to support their party’s nominee on Election Day, with massive implications for who controls the Senate majority next year. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Republican Ken Paxton are both trying to stitch their parties back together for battleground races after divisive primaries. Two focus groups — one with Michiganders who supported Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ unsuccessful Senate bid, and another with Texans who backed Republican Sen. John Cornyn in that primary — reveal how some rank-and-file voters are struggling to process personal concerns about the nominees alongside a desire to be loyal to their party. The focus groups, produced by Syracuse University and the research firms Engagious and Sago and observed by NBC News, showed Cornyn voters who see Paxton as corrupt but are hesitant to hand Democrats a Senate seat. In Michigan, the Stevens voters worried about whether El-Sayed is too extreme — and some said they were concerned about his Muslim faith and his allegiances. Both narratives echo how their general election opponents — former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, and state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas — have sought to define them. “I’m split down the middle. In this instance, I really feel that I am looking at the lesser of two evils and I’m not sure which that is,” said Kathleen S., a 62-year-old Republican from Comal County in Texas. Unlike a poll, which uses statistical methods to demonstrate how a larger population feels, focus groups dig into deeper detail about how a handful of people feel about key questions. In these two 90-minute conversations, the Cornyn voters were more open to looking past ethical concerns about Paxton, the Texas attorney general. The Stevens voters, meanwhile, included more political independents, and they were more hesitant to back El-Sayed, a former public health official in Michigan. “In Michigan, I heard undecided Stevens voters growing nervous with El-Sayed, and in Texas I heard Cornyn voters abandoning their preferred candidate, Talarico, in order to put loyalty to the GOP first,” said Rich Thau, president of Engagious, who moderated the groups. “These undecided voters truly contorted themselves as they struggled to justify a choice they feared they’d later regret.” Worries about El-Sayed The group of seven Stevens primary voters were not dyed-in-the-wool Democrats. The group included five independents (four of whom voted for President Donald Trump in 2024) and two Democrats. Their hesitance about El-Sayed may reflect how general election swing voters are digesting their choice, rather than the Democratic base. But overall, only two of those seven said they were leaning toward voting for El-Sayed. The two Democratic voters split between El-Sayed and Rogers. Stevens herself has endorsed El-Sayed. Isaac W., a 29-year-old Democrat from Oakland County who voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, said he is leaning toward Rogers but hopes other states deliver a Democratic-controlled Senate. Isaac views an El-Sayed victory as “almost inevitable” and is hoping to send a message with his vote that El-Sayed’s brand of politics isn’t as popular with voters as other Democrats like Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is running for governor. “I want people to see when they look at the election results that El-Sayed was running far behind Benson, so they can see that a normal Democrat is going to be the better choice for most things, and that a young, charismatic, slippery politician who will flirt with extremists and not answer questions is not going to succeed as well,” he said. Isaac said El-Sayed has addressed his top concern, the “existential risk” prompted by the rise in artificial intelligence, and he understands that more Democratic votes in the Senate would push back on Trump, whose administration he described as corrupt. But while criticizing El-Sayed as too extreme, Isaac praised Rogers’ recent decision to break with Trump on tariffs, saying it helped to change his mind about the Republican. “Up to that point, I thought he was just a lockstep Republican following Trump’s lead like all the rest of them, but then he was willing to say what is true and obvious, and I respect him for that,” he said. Danny S., a 64-year-old Democrat, disagreed and emphatically backed El-Sayed. “He seems more transparent than Rogers does. I think Rogers is just jumping on, just an opportunist,” he said, before adding that Rogers “didn’t do nothing last time,” a reference to the Republican’s seven-term stint in the House that ended in 2014. Four of the five pro-Stevens independents said they’re leaning toward backing Rogers. They felt El-Sayed was too extreme, echoing the message that Rogers and his allies have spent tens of millions of dollars to hammer on the airwaves. “El-Sayed would never get my vote. He’s way too extremist and we don’t need another extremist in Washington, D.C., especially from the Democratic Party that I used to belong to. I just think Rogers is a better candidate,” said Heather S., a 52-year-old independent who voted for Trump in 2024. Brittany E., a 36-year-old independent who also voted for Trump, said that while she had previously been leaning toward El-Sayed, she’s since shifted more toward Rogers because she isn’t sure if El-Sayed can be effective. She went on to add that El-Sayed has spent so much of the campaign defending himself from attacks that she isn’t sure what he believes or “how he’s going to make change.” “I would just tell him to be more honest and open to criticism without anger,” she said. A handful of these voters repeatedly questioned whether El-Sayed would adequately represent all of Michigan — like Michael D., a 51-year-old independent voter who backed Harris in 2024 but is now leaning toward Rogers. “I think he’s kind of, I don’t want to say an extremist because he’s not. I think his just views are not basically representative of this entire party,” he said. “I think it’s because it’s more focused on one particular group where it’s not just basically the everybody,” Michael D. said, later clarifying that he was referring to Muslim Americans Michael D. was not the only voter to suggest that El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if elected, would not represent all Michiganders Heather S., a 52-year-old independent who voted for Trump in 2024, said she’s supporting Rogers because she believes he’s “not as extreme” and “even though he is a Trumpster, that maybe he can bring something else to the party, be able to work with both parties.” “I think El-Sayed would just represent Dearborn,” she said, referencing the Michigan city with a significant Muslim population. “I’m not racist. El-Sayed, he comes across as he just wants to represent the Muslims and not the whole Michigan community — not even just the Democratic Party, just the Muslim community,” she said. She then added: “We all need him if he gets in there. And he could unify us, but I don’t think he can. He’s too extreme and he’s going to spend most of his time fighting to unify us, and it’ll be a waste of time.” Others took issue with that framing, including Kimberly C., a 54-year-old independent who voted for Trump but says she’s leaning toward El-Sayed this year. “I think that people stop short with him because he’s Muslim and they’re not looking beyond that viewpoint, or when they look at him,” she said. “It’s the same thing for me as in 2024 when Kamala Harris ran, and to me, it felt like so many people didn’t want to vote for her just because she was Black,” Kimberly C. continued. “So I think we need to look beyond the racism and prejudice and try to unify the country.” Partisan pull toward Paxton In Texas, the mostly Republican group of participants who had supported Cornyn in the GOP primary were much more inclined to toe the party line. “It’s clear if they were voting based on candidate quality these voters would favor Talarico. But their preference for and loyalty to the Republican Party or differences with Democrats is the bigger differentiator,” Margaret Talev, director of the Institute for Democracy, Journalism and Citizenship at Syracuse University, which hosts the focus group project. The panel included five Republicans, with two planning to support Paxton and two leaning his way, while one was leaning toward backing Talarico. The lone independent voter in the panel is planning to support Talarico, as well. The Republicans, in particular, wrestled with Paxton’s past controversies. He was impeached in 2023 on bribery and corruption charges and ultimately acquitted. In 2015, he was indicted on charges related to securities fraud and avoided a trial after reaching an agreement with prosecutors. He is also going through a divorce, with his wife saying she was separating from him on “biblical grounds.” But for some of them, allegiance to their political party trumped those scandals. All five Republicans in the panel said they would back Talarico if he was a Republican, underscoring how their party affiliation loomed large. “Right now I’m embarrassed of saying [I will vote] Republican, because Paxton has so many skeletons in his closet. And I just can’t make myself jump the fence and go to the other party,” said Ruth L., a 63-year-old Republican from Tarrant County. Asked for her message to Talarico as he tries to win her vote, Ruth said, “Change parties.” Steve F., a 67-year-old Republican from Collin County, said he was planning to back Paxton “mostly because of the party,” voicing concerns about the GOP losing control of the Senate. “Talarico as a Democrat, he doesn’t share my same values. At least the party doesn’t share my values,” Steve said, noting he had concerns about Talarico’s past comments on immigration and gender. “I do respect him as a person. I think he has a lot of integrity.” Others were still unsure about Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator who shot to prominence this election cycle. Kathleen S., the Republican who was torn between Talarico and Paxton as a choice between “the lesser of two evils,” described Paxton as “very corrupt” and raised concerns that Talarico is saying what voters want to hear. “If it was today, I would probably pick Paxton because I would rather go with the evil I know than the evil I don’t,” she said. But not everyone was leaning toward Paxton. Greg D., a 48-year-old Republican who supported Trump in 2024, said he is leaning toward supporting Talarico. “Let’s change it up, get something different,” he said. “I mean, we’ve kind of done that. We went back to the old with Trump, so just maybe some new fresh blood, get in there and do something different.” Greg D. also noted he listens to Joe Rogan’s podcast. While Greg did not connect Talarico and Rogan, Talarico did appear on the podcast in 2025, impressing the host so much that Rogan encouraged Talarico to run for president. The lone independent voter, Danielle S. from Collin County, said she “begrudgingly” voted for Harris in 2024 and voted in the GOP Senate primary this year because she saw the race as more important. She said that even though she herself is not religious, she was also drawn to how Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, talks about Christianity. “Talarico is, from what I know, what I’ve seen, what I’ve listened to, integrity on legs. Pretty much the opposite of what Ken Paxton is. He’s not a man of integrity,” Danielle S. said of her decision to support the Democrat.

articles.title: US lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods before midterm elections
articles.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.

Starting on 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment," the White House said on Friday.

Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.

The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (£15bn) of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".

Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

The White House said while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".

It said the action reflected President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".

In a statement to the BBC, Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.

Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally, and largest trading partner".

She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.

Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.

Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a ⁠trade ​deal with the US.

Carney, for his part, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC.

LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

articles.title: Why is Trump questioning Ilhan Omar’s name?
articles.summary: A Justice Department filing listed a different name for her, prompting Trump to call for her resignation.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has called for Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar to resign from the US Congress, reviving allegations of identity fraud after a court filing identified the Minnesota politician by an additional name.

The DOJ filing, submitted on Wednesday, refers to Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar” – “a/k/a” is an abbreviation for “also known as”.

The document filed by the administration does not establish that Omar committed fraud.

In response to allegations that Ilhan Omar is not her real name, the lawmaker posted on X, “So let’s make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar”.

The controversy follows a federal investigation into Omar’s immigration history and a search of her Washington, DC, home on October 12.

Omar has said she plans to move out of the home , citing safety concerns.

October 12: Federal agents search Omar’s home

Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington, DC, residence under a “judicially authorised search warrant” as part of an ongoing criminal investigation. It reportedly concerns allegations that Omar or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork when the family fled Somalia and came to the United States in 1995, when she was a child. Omar has denied wrongdoing and described the search as political intimidation.

October 15: Requests to unseal court records

Judicial Watch and The New York Times, alongside 14 other press organisations, filed applications in the US District Court for the District of Columbia seeking access to sealed records related to the search warrant. Judicial Watch said it wanted the warrant, supporting affidavits and an inventory of seized materials made public.

October 21: Justice Department filing identifies Omar by another name

In a motion seeking additional time to respond to the requests for records, the Justice Department referred to the congresswoman as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar”.

The filing did not explain the relationship between the names. Instead, prosecutors asked the court to delay their response until after they fully executed the search warrant. The government said it would submit a status report within 30 days of completing the search.

October 22: Name allegations become public, Trump calls for resignation

Fox News Digital cited the court filing and reported that unnamed sources said that Omar’s birth name was Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. The article prompted renewed speculation about her name and longstanding rumours concerning her 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Some have claimed he is Omar’s brother, an allegation she has repeatedly denied.

President Trump publicly escalated his attacks on Omar, calling for her resignation as the name controversy spread. He has presented the alternative name listed in the court filing as evidence of fraud, even though the filing makes no such finding and she has not been charged with any criminal offences.

October 23: Representative Omar responds

A spokesperson for Omar told Al Jazeera in a statement: “The Congresswoman’s name has always been Ilhan Omar. Any indication otherwise is flat out false”.

Omar also rejected the allegations in a post on X, accusing Trump of promoting conspiracy theories through the Justice Department.

“Whenever the news turns bad, this creep reaches for one name: mine. So let’s make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar,” she added, before telling Trump to focus on “what your VP’s real name is”.

Muslim American candidates face attacks over their names

In an interview with MS NOW’s Chris Hayes, Omar argued that the attacks were intended to drive her out of Congress, saying her critics believed someone of her background and faith “shouldn’t be in Congress” or hold a position influencing US law.

“I have a legal right to be a member of Congress, and I am honoured,” she said.

The scrutiny of Omar’s name comes amid a wider wave of attacks on Muslim American politicians, including Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan.

In an interview with Al Jazeera on Thursday, a Michigan voter questioned why El-Sayed does not use his “real name”, seemingly referring to his full name.

“Abdul’s barely out there. He doesn’t even say his real name. Like, why can’t you share your real name?” the voter said. When asked if she knew the full name of El-Sayed’s Republican opponent Mike Rogers, she said, “Mohamed’s not his middle name”.

El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, has faced attacks on his Arab heritage and Muslim faith during his Senate campaign. Trump has mocked his name and called him a “jihadist”. Trump also said at a rally that he could call El-Sayed “Mohammed”, adding that he could call him “whatever the hell I want”.

The U.S. Secret Service and D.C. police are investigating reports of a “suspicious item” near the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which resulted in a road closure.

“Around 2:40 p.m., on October 23, 2026, Secret Service Police were notified of a suspicious item near 17th St. and Pennsylvania Avenue,” according to a statement from a Secret Service spokesperson to The Hill’s partner network NewsNation.

Out of an “abundance of caution,” the roads were closed in the area, the statement said.

The Metropolitan Police Department and other partners responded to the scene, according to the statement. It is an ongoing investigation.

The Embassy of Ireland, located in the same area, said it is “currently closed due to an ongoing security incident in the area, which has resulted in a number of street closures,” in a post on social platform X .

“Citizens in the area should heed the advice of local authorities,” the post said.

Earlier today in a similar incident , authorities investigated reports of a suspicious package near the Ukrainian Embassy. The embassy was evacuated before it reopened later as the item was deemed not harmful.

articles.title: Disappointed primary voters weigh their choices: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman have the key takeaways from our latest voter focus groups in Michigan and Texas. Plus, Kristen Welker dives into the downballot effects of this cycle’s key gubernatorial races. — Adam Wollner Focus groups: Their candidates lost in the Michigan and Texas primaries. Now what? By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Some voters who backed losing candidates in two key Senate primaries this year are still wrestling with whether to support their party’s nominee on Election Day, with major implications for who controls the Senate majority next year. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Republican Ken Paxton are both trying to stitch their parties back together for their battleground races after divisive primaries. Two focus groups — one with Michiganders who supported Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ unsuccessful Senate bid, and another with Texans who backed Republican Sen. John Cornyn in that primary — reveal how some rank-and-file voters are struggling to process personal concerns about the nominees alongside a desire to be loyal to their party. The focus groups, produced by Syracuse University and the research firms Engagious and Sago and observed by NBC News, showed Cornyn voters who see Paxton as corrupt but are hesitant to hand Democrats a Senate seat. In Michigan, the Stevens voters worried about whether El-Sayed is too extreme — and some voiced concerns about his Muslim faith and his allegiances. Both narratives echo how their general election opponents — former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, and state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas — have sought to define them. “I’m split down the middle. In this instance, I really feel that I am looking at the lesser of two evils and I’m not sure which that is,” said Kathleen S., a 62-year-old Republican from Comal County in Texas. In these two 90-minute conversations, the Cornyn voters were more open to looking past ethical concerns about Paxton, the Texas attorney general. The Stevens voters, meanwhile, included more political independents, and they were more hesitant to back El-Sayed, a former public health official in Michigan. “In Michigan, I heard undecided Stevens voters growing nervous with El-Sayed, and in Texas I heard Cornyn voters abandoning their preferred candidate, Talarico, in order to put loyalty to the GOP first,” said Rich Thau, the president of Engagious, who moderated the groups. “These undecided voters truly contorted themselves as they struggled to justify a choice they feared they’d later regret.” Read more → Ramaswamy ad underscores how governor’s races could affect downballot contests Analysis by Kristen Welker The impact of Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad against Democratic opponent Amy Acton could be felt well beyond the governor’s race. The ad features Acton’s estranged mother accusing her of lying. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother in decades and that she was sexually abused by her mother’s husband when she was a child. But while Ramaswamy and some of his allies defend the spot, the flood of other Republicans condemning it — including Sen. Jon Husted, who is on the November ballot as well — emphasizes how the controversy could have a ripple effect downballot. One GOP strategist told me there are concerns within the party that the ad could turn off critical women voters in Husted’s race and multiple competitive House districts in the state. Ohio isn’t the only state where the top-of-the-ticket contests could shift the dynamics in races farther down the ballot. Pennsylvania has at least four battleground House races this year, and Democratic candidates could get a boost from Gov. Josh Shapiro as he runs for re-election. Shapiro’s contest against Republican Stacy Garrity is not expected to be very competitive, even in the perennial swing state, given his high approval ratings. But he’s been focusing intently on boosting downballot candidates, cutting ads and hitting the campaign trail. Starting tomorrow, Shapiro is going on a 10-day bus tour across the state. Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper appears to be pulling away from Republican Michael Whatley in the North Carolina Senate race, which could help Democrats hold the state’s uber-competitive 1st District, and maybe even flip the redder 11th District. It’s a similar case in Arizona, where Democrats hope a strong showing by Gov. Katie Hobbs can help them in the 1st and 6th districts, both perennial battlegrounds, and in their push to defeat Rep. Eli Crane in a district Donald Trump won by about 15 points in 2024. In Iowa, where Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates are running strong, Republicans have already retreated from the 1st District. In the 3rd District, Republican Rep. Zach Nunn is running a new ad aimed squarely at winning over Democrats. And Democrats are flooding millions of dollars into the 2nd District, which Trump won by 10 points in 2024. The fiercely competitive Texas gubernatorial and Senate races, as well as the closer-than-expected Florida governor’s race, have significant downballot implications in two states Republicans made central to their redistricting push. Republicans have shifted resources away from their bid to defeat Rep. Henry Cuellar, while Democrats are eyeing the redrawn 15th and 35th districts, both of which Trump won by double digits in 2024. And both sides have been pouring money into the seats Florida Republicans redrew to their benefit. Republicans have a few top-of-the ticket dynamics breaking their way, too. They’re hopeful New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s strong campaign can help former Republican Sen. John Sununu in his Senate race. And in Georgia, the tens of millions of dollars Republican Rick Jackson has poured into his campaign for governor could be felt in other races on the state’s ballot. Races for Senate and governor could also have down-ticket effects in Michigan, where multiple House races are in play. We’ll dive into the latest in those Michigan contests on “Meet the Press” this Sunday, with exclusive interviews with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., and our chief data analyst Steve Kornacki will also join me. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: How will Democrats address UFO sightings if returned to the majority?
articles.summary: Unidentified flying objects (UFOs) have long captivated Americans — a majority of whom, recent polling suggests, believe the government is hiding information about the phenomena. And the debate has also made its way to Capitol Hill. In recent years, conversations surrounding UFOs, which the government now refers to as unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAPs), have heated…
articles.body:
Unidentified flying objects (UFOs) have long captivated Americans — a majority of whom , recent polling suggests, believe the government is hiding information about the phenomena. And the debate has also made its way to Capitol Hill.

In recent years, conversations surrounding UFOs, which the government now refers to as unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAPs), have heated up on both sides of the congressional political aisle.

In 2022, under a Democratic majority, a House Intelligence subcommittee held the first congressional hearing on UFOs in over five decades. Two officials leading the Pentagon’s UAP task force testified, with one making clear they were encouraging pilots to report sightings.

Americans still remain distrustful of the government’s handling of these phenomena. An August Gallup poll found that, while nearly half of Americans are skeptical that UFOs are of extraterrestrial origin, 78 percent believe the government knows more about the sightings than it tells the public.

In line with the public’s fascination, the second Trump administration has declassified files on UFOs and created a new governance board to coordinate investigations into reports of sightings.

Some lawmakers have taken an active role in calling for government transparency on the topic. And, with Democrats likely to take back control of the House next year, The Hill has broken down how the party’s UFO clarity advocates may address investigations and declassifications.

Democratic leadership has previously backed efforts to increase transparency surrounding federal UFO investigations. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), Democrats’ likely House speaker choice should the party reclaim the lower chamber and current Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) step down, said in 2023 he supported sharing data on the phenomena with the public whenever feasible.

“I do support transparency to the extent this information that can be put into the public domain that is enlightening, one way or the other, and perhaps is able to dismiss some of the conspiracy theories that exist increasingly in our society,” Jeffries said in July 2023, as reported by The Hill’s broadcasting partner, NewsNation.

But Congress also has a caucus already dedicated to investigating and declassifying UFO information.

In 2023, Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) founded the UAP Caucus, which currently includes himself as well as Reps. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), Eric Burlison (R-Mo.) and Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.).

The caucus is “dedicated to the study, disclosure, and policy development surrounding” UFOs, according to its website , and hopes to expand the group to include the Senate.

Moskowitz is the caucus’s only Democrat, and he is in a tough battle for reelection after Florida Republicans redrew the state’s congressional districts. Two more members are set to leave the caucus, as Mace is retiring and Ogles lost renomination .

But the caucus also includes “honorable mentions” — members, including senators, who are not technically part of the caucus but are “instrumental” in supporting its goals.

‘Honorable mention’ Democrats support the cause

The Hill reached out to House Democrats running for reelection who are listed as either members or “honorable mentions” of the UAP Caucus.

Rep. Andre Carson (D-Ind.), one of the caucus’s honorable mentions, accused the Trump administration in a statement sent to The Hill of having “slow walked” UFO reporting and investigation transparency efforts. He specifically singled out a “historical UAP record report” and called for its immediate release.

“I’m calling for the immediate release of this report, which is expected to provide additional findings of historical military and intelligence investigations of UAP, including how incidents were investigated, the role of classified programs, and whether relevant activities were appropriately disclosed to Congress,” Carson said .

During the 2022 House hearing, Carson pushed to destigmatize UFO reporting for pilots and other military officials. The Indiana Democrat said at the time the stigma around the phenomena had “gotten in the way of good intelligence reporting,” as he alleged some pilots “were laughed at” when the reported unidentified aircraft.

Carson is a member of the House Intelligence Committee. Other House Democrats on the UAP Caucus “honorable mentions” list include Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), Ro Khanna (Calif.) and Jamie Raskin (Md.).

articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts Ohio governor’s race from toss-up to lean Democrat
articles.summary: The Cook Political Report is shifting a closely watched gubernatorial contest toward Democrats after a controversial campaign ad shook up the race. The nonpartisan election forecaster moved the governor’s race in Ohio from “toss up” to “lean Democrat,” now favoring Amy Acton (D) to beat Vivek Ramaswamy (R) in the Buckeye State. The race was…
articles.body:
The Cook Political Report is shifting a closely watched gubernatorial contest toward Democrats after a controversial campaign ad shook up the race.

The nonpartisan election forecaster moved the governor’s race in Ohio from “toss up” to “lean Democrat,” now favoring Amy Acton (D) to beat Vivek Ramaswamy (R) in the Buckeye State.

The race was the source of national attention after Ramaswamy debuted an ad with Acton’s estranged mother, who claims Acton is a “liar” and encourages voters not to elect her as Ohio governor.

Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12. Her campaign said that she was sexually abused by her stepfather, who her mother remained with until his death.

The ad was widely condemned by Democrats and even some Republicans , including current Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R). Still, President Trump and Vice President Vance have both vehemently defended the ad.

Jessica Taylor, Cook Political Report’s Senate and governor’s editor, wrote in her analysis that Republicans they have talked to do not think the ad was a smart move.

“We haven’t talked to a GOP source who thought this was a good idea,” Taylor wrote. “This is not the kind of TV ad you run if you’re winning — or even if you’re confident you can. Recent polls were trending in Acton’s direction even before the bombshell ad became a national news story.”

Cook conducted a poll of the Ohio gubernatorial race before the ad was released and found Acton leading Ramaswamy by five points. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, another nonpartisan election forecaster, also changed its rating from “toss up” to “leans Democratic” earlier this week.

Acton’s fundraising has surged since the release of the ad, which Ramaswamy’s campaign is now spending $4 million to put on the air.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Acton a 62 percent chance of victory.

Trump uses DPA to give $150M for gas and diesel

President Trump invoked the Defense Production Act on Thursday night, announcing that the government would be spending $150 million toward boosting domestic gas and diesel production as the White House looks to ease consumer pain at the gas pump.

The announcement was made in a presidential memorandum Thursday, but the president detailed the exact amount of spending expected during a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa.

The Cold War-era law gives the president broad powers to increase production of resources within the U.S. for national defense purposes.

The Energy Department in a press release noted that the injection of cash was “expected to increase U.S. refining output by millions of gallons per day.”

Meanwhile, Trump’s memo, directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to implement it, “ including making necessary purchases, commitments, and financial instruments to enable” oil-related projects.

articles.body:
US officially doubles last year’s measles numbers

The U.S. has officially doubled the number of measles cases it saw in 2025 according to the most up-to-date information from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), marking the worst year the country has seen by far in terms of disease transmission.

As of the CDC’s update on Friday, the U.S. has confirmed 4,588 measles cases this year across 47 jurisdictions and 42 new outbreaks, compared to 2025’s total of 2,289 confirmed cases.

Though the CDC has recognized three measles deaths this year, Pennsylvania alone has reported five. Local authorities reported a sixth death, but it’s currently under investigation.

The state reported 1,338 cases across 44 counties — nearly 30 percent of the nationwide total.

The CDC reports that 96 percent of cases occurred among people who were unvaccinated or had unknown immunization statuses. The majority of infections, 59 percent, have occurred among people aged 19 and younger .

While official numbers indicate nearly 7,000 cases have been recorded since the start of 2025, when measles transmission began worsening, infectious disease experts speculate that a significant portion of cases have gone underreported.

Andy Pavia, pediatric infectious disease epidemiologist at the University of Utah, said at the annual IDWeek infectious disease conference this week that the true total since last year is “probably greater than 20,000.”

“We’re up against enormous odds,” said Pavia. “Our politicians are waging warfare and lawfare against public health, against vaccines, against science, and against essentially our patients’ best interests.”

While federal leadership has given soft, tacit support for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, members of the Trump administration have also continued to cast doubt on the safety of the shot .

Earlier this year, President Trump signed an executive to split up the doses of the MMR vaccine, claiming without evidence that the combined vaccine that’s been around since 1971 can be “quite lethal.”

articles.body:
A new poll released Friday suggests half of Americans are concerned Republicans may try to overturn the results of November’s midterm election.

Fifty percent of respondents to the New York Times/Siena University survey said they were either “very” or “somewhat worried” the GOP may use “illegal means” to overturn the election, compared to 49 percent who are either “not too worried” or “not at all worried.”

A strong majority of Democrats — 86 percent — were among the share of likely voters who reported feeling worry about potential GOP election interference, and 52 percent independents felt the same. Even 10 percent of Republicans say they are worried their own party would overturn the results.

NYT/Siena also asked respondents if they feared Democrats may overturn the results, and 31 percent said they were — a group mainly consisting of Republicans.

Still, similar shares of Democratic, Republican and independents respondents to the NYT/Siena poll said they trusted midterm results would be accurate. And, across all parties, likely voters’ trust reached 74 percent.

President Trump has pushed claims of voter fraud for years, mainly when he or his party loses. Courts and election officials have consistently debunked or found no evidence for claims of widespread fraud in U.S. elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters Thursday the Justice Department (DOJ) has no intention “to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.” However, he did not rule out the potential for the DOJ to intervene in or block states from verifying election results.

O n Friday morning, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

The DOJ argued that, because another candidate with the same name is on the ballot, the election is not fair and could confuse voters. Sen. Sullivan is identified on the ballot with his Republican and incumbent status to differentiate himself from the other Dan Sullivan.

The poll was conducted Oct. 12-19 among 3,494 likely voters nationwide. The margin of error is 1.9 percentage points
